source.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
source.authors: Curt Tigges; Michael Hanna; Qi-Nan Yu; Stella Biderman

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether an identifiable algorithm remains consistent across training checkpoints and model scales, using circuit and path-patching analyses rather than the original grokking setup.
record.gate_note: The paper measures task performance and circuit development during Pythia pretraining, but does not measure training-versus-test accuracy gaps, grokking delays, or their dependence on training-set size. Its evidence for algorithm consistency concerns the IOI circuit.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 in a new setting, decoder-only LLM pretraining rather than small algorithmic tasks. Path patching checks whether the same IOI algorithm (name-mover/copy-suppression, S-inhibition, induction/duplicate-token steps) is used across Pythia models from 160M to 2.8B parameters. It measures no delayed generalization, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The record's T2 is better read as T3, since this is not the grokking setup.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely correct. The authors conclude that the IOI algorithm stays stable over training despite component turnover and is broadly similar across Pythia scales, with a small component difference at 160m. They add that circuit size grows with model size and node sets can fluctuate. They caution that the results may not hold for more complex tasks or other model families.
record.recipe_differences: This is a longitudinal circuit-analysis study of pretrained Pythia language models on behavioral tasks, not training small networks on small algorithmic datasets to study delayed generalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Individual attention-head identities and functional scores can change over training; the IOI circuit also differs slightly across model scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Within one training run, the attention heads filling a role change: name-mover head (4,6) stops at ~3e10 tokens and other heads take over. Task performance and the algorithm metrics stay stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuit component identities drift over long pretraining while the implemented algorithm stays stable (load-balancing / self-repair).

fits_no_version.finding: Task abilities and functional heads emerge at similar token counts across model sizes (name movers at 2–8e9 tokens; induction heads after ~2e9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability and component emergence timing is roughly scale-invariant in Pythia pretraining.

record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Representation Learning for NLP (metadata); the paper text also identifies NeurIPS 2024.
record.problems: The IOI algorithm analysis covers only one task and one model family; Pythia-70m was omitted because it did not learn IOI, and Pythia-6.9b/12b were omitted from circuit analysis. Larger-model checkpoints were sampled at approximately one third of the available checkpoints. Relevant metric values are plotted rather than stated numerically, and the paper itself cautions that results may not generalize to more complex tasks or other model families.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested V6 algorithm-consistency claim were left out.

untested.parts: Convergence across random seeds, across different architectures or model families, and across optimizer or other hyperparameter changes. Only model size varies, and all Pythia models share data, architecture and training recipe. Pythia-6.9b and 12b were not analysed; Pythia-70m does not learn IOI. No algorithmic task such as modular addition was used.
LLM pretraining is studied, but no train/test gap or delayed generalization is measured.
No small algorithmic datasets, train/test accuracy, or training-set-size sweep.
No grokking circuit or memorization-removal analysis.
No weight-decay, critical dataset size, or ungrokking experiment.

missing.what: Circuit size (node count) correlates with model size: Pearson r=0.72 for IOI and SVA, 0.9 for Greater-Than, 0.6 for Gendered Pronoun. Larger models use more heads in the same roles. This qualifies 'same algorithm' at the implementation level.
Node-set Jaccard similarity over training is more volatile for smaller models (70m, 160m), and Gendered-Pronoun circuits can change late in training.

record.verdict_notes: This study sits outside the grokking setting. Its link to V6 rests on reading 'same task, same algorithm' as including LLM sub-task circuits across model scale. The scale comparison is confounded by Pythia's shared data, architecture and recipe. All key metric values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: No small algorithmic training datasets, training-accuracy saturation, chance-level test accuracy, delayed test-accuracy rise, or training-set-size sweep.
No grokking circuit, Fourier algorithm for modular arithmetic, or analysis of memorizing components being removed as generalization develops.
No comparison of training regimes, initialization-scale or weight-norm intervention, or lazy-to-rich transition as a cause of grokking-like delays.
The paper studies LLM pretraining on realistic data, but does not measure delayed generalization or a grokking-like train/test accuracy gap.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking experiment.
Tests IOI algorithm consistency across Pythia sizes 160M–2.8B and training checkpoints, not across different architectures, training families, or hyperparameter settings.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact investigation.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m
rows.operation_detail: Path-patching metric for the contribution of copy-suppression and name-mover heads to IOI performance.
rows.measure: Percent of model IOI performance explained by copy-suppression/name-mover heads
rows.baseline: Reference is the ablation effect of all components that could affect the relevant receivers; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Figure only; the text says core solver scores are above 70% and scores are generally above 50%.
rows.note: The authors report that this metric remains stable after circuit formation and that there are no dramatic algorithm shifts.
rows.check: R1–R12 each plot one model's metric over its own checkpoints. Stability within one run is not what V6 names (convergence across runs). These rows bear on V6 only because the same high metrics hold in all four model sizes. Researchers should read the V6 evidence as the cross-scale comparison, not the over-time stability. All values are figure-only: generally above 50%, and above 70% for the core solver heads.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m
rows.operation_detail: Compared IOI circuit components across model scales.

conditions.value: end-of-training circuits across Pythia-160m to Pythia-2.8b

rows.measure: Presence of duplicate-token heads in the identified IOI algorithm
rows.baseline: Other model circuits in the comparison include duplicate-token heads.
rows.value: The Pythia-160m circuit does not involve duplicate-token heads.
rows.note: The paper reports broad algorithmic similarity, but also this component-level difference; it describes these as small differences amid overall similarity.
rows.check: The state is correct. The baseline should say that 410m, 1.4b and 2.8b circuits include duplicate-token heads, and the 160m circuit does not. The name-mover, copy-suppression and S-inhibition steps are shared by all models.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, cross-scale comparison immediately following Figure 4 discussion.

relationships.condition: IOI task, Pythia-160m, 410m, 1.4b and 2.8b after the circuit forms
relationships.reason: The same three-step IOI algorithm explains most of the effect in every size: scores generally above 50%, core solver heads above 70% (R1–R12).
relationships.display_finding: The shared three-step algorithm generally scored above 50% across sizes, with core solver heads scoring above 70%.

source_check.condition: IOI task, Pythia-160m, 410m, 1.4b and 2.8b after the circuit forms
source_check.reason: R1–R12 jointly support recurrence of the three-step IOI account across sizes: scores generally exceed 50%, and core solver scores exceed 70%. Support concerns shared algorithmic structure within Pythia.

relationships.condition: Component-level comparison of end-of-training IOI circuits across Pythia scales
relationships.reason: Pythia-160m's circuit lacks the duplicate-token heads used by the larger models, so the same algorithm holds only at the coarse level (R13).
relationships.display_finding: Pythia-160m lacked the duplicate-token heads used by larger models despite sharing the coarse indirect-object identification algorithm.
